strings.notes: Iterating over a string with for (traversal, looping and counting characters, py4e 6 / MIT L4) belongs to B04 for_loops / loop_patterns, which run in parallel and should encompass strings.length_and_membership and string_indexing_slicing.index_characters. String equality and ordering are owned by B02 comparison_operators. \n and \t are B01 print_output.newlines_and_tabs (non-core, so encompassed rather than required). Regular expressions are a later batch and can use strings.multiline_and_raw for raw strings.

string_concatenation.notes: Building strings inside loops (accumulating with +=) belongs to B04 loop_patterns, which should encompass join_with_plus. f-strings are the preferred alternative and live in string_formatting.

string_indexing_slicing.notes: Taught before list slicing; B06 list_slicing should list these topics as prerequisites and teach only what differs for lists (slice assignment, copying). Looping over indexes with range(len(s)) is B04.

string_methods.notes: split() returns a list; lists themselves are B06, which should encompass split_into_parts and join_pieces. Loops over split() results and over lines of a file are B04/B10. Alignment methods (center/ljust/rjust/zfill) are covered by f-string specs in string_formatting.width_and_alignment and not given their own topic. partition(), casefold() and dir(str)/help(str) were left out; B05 builtin_functions may add method discovery.

string_formatting.notes: f"{x=}" for debugging belongs to B09 debugging. print(sep=, end=) is B01 print_output.sep_and_end. Format specs for dates are B13 datetime.

string_immutability.notes: One topic, as the evidence is three 'introduced' mentions. The general mutable/immutable distinction and aliasing of lists is B06 mutability_aliasing, which should encompass this topic.

unicode_encoding.notes: Both topics are supplemental. File encodings (open(..., encoding='utf-8')) belong to B10 file_io; bytes from the network to the web batch. A full Caesar cipher over a whole message needs a loop and belongs to B04/B05 practice.

topics.title: String values and quotes
topics.summary: Store text in a variable as a string, put quotes inside strings, and escape quotes and backslashes.

knowledge_points.title: A string is text in quotes, stored like any value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
greeting = "Hello"
empty = ""
print(greeting, type(greeting))
# Hello <class 'str'>
"" is the empty string: a string with no characters.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of short programs that store and print strings; pick which values are strings.

knowledge_points.title: Quotes inside a string: use the other kind outside
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("It's late")
print('She said "hi"')
# It's late
# She said "hi"
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the outer quotes that make a given sentence a valid string; write a print for a sentence with an apostrophe.

knowledge_points.title: Escaping with a backslash: \' \" and \\
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print('It\'s late')
print("C:\\temp")
# It's late
# C:\temp
A backslash plus the next character is one escape: \' is a quote, \\ is one backslash.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what strings with escapes print; fill in the escape needed to print a quote or a backslash.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: an apostrophe ends the string early
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print('It's late')   # SyntaxError: the string ends after It
Fix: print("It's late") or print('It\'s late')
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the quoting error in one-line prints.

topics.title: Multi-line strings and raw strings
topics.summary: Write strings that span several lines with triple quotes, and keep backslashes literal with raw strings.

knowledge_points.title: Triple quotes span several lines
knowledge_points.worked_example:
poem = """Roses are red,
violets are blue."""
print(poem)
# Roses are red,
# violets are blue.
The line break typed in the code is part of the string.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed lines of a triple-quoted string; write one that prints a 3-line address.

knowledge_points.title: Triple-quoted text keeps every newline and space
knowledge_points.worked_example:
text = """
    hi
"""
print(text)
# (empty line)
#     hi
# (empty line)
The newline right after the opening quotes, the indentation and the final newline are all kept.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many lines (including blank ones) a triple-quoted string prints and where the spaces go.

knowledge_points.title: Backslashes in Windows paths surprise you
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("C:\new\table")
# C:
# ew<TAB>able
\n and \t were read as escapes. Fix: "C:\\new\\table"
knowledge_points.practice: Spot which backslashes form escapes in a string; fix paths that print wrongly.

knowledge_points.title: Raw strings r"..." keep backslashes as typed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(r"C:\new\table")
# C:\new\table
The r prefix turns escapes off; useful for paths and, later, regular expressions.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output with and without the r prefix; choose where a raw string avoids a bug.

topics.title: Length of a string and the in operator
topics.summary: Count characters with len() and test whether one string appears inside another with in and not in.

knowledge_points.title: len() counts characters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len("hello"))     # 5
print(len("hi there"))  # 8: the space counts
print(len(""))          # 0
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() of strings with spaces, punctuation and the empty string.

knowledge_points.title: Escapes count as one character
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len("a\nb"))   # 3
print(len("\\"))     # 1
What you type is not what is stored: \n is one character.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() for strings containing escapes and stored in variables.

knowledge_points.title: in tests for a substring
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("cat" in "concatenate")   # True
print("dog" in "concatenate")   # False
print("" in "abc")              # True: the empty string is in every string
knowledge_points.practice: Predict True/False for in tests on words and sentences; write an expression that checks for '@' in an email.

knowledge_points.title: not in, and in is case-sensitive
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Cat" in "concatenate")   # False: C is not c
print("x" not in "abc")         # True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results with mixed case and not in; fix a check that misses a capitalised word.

topics.title: Joining strings with +
topics.summary: Build new strings with + and +=, adding the spaces yourself, and tell + apart from commas in print.

knowledge_points.title: + glues two strings into one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
word = "snow" + "man"
print(word)   # snowman
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of joining 2-3 string literals and variables.

knowledge_points.title: Spaces do not appear by themselves
knowledge_points.worked_example:
first = "Ada"
last = "Lovelace"
print(first + " " + last)   # Ada Lovelace
print(first + last)         # AdaLovelace
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the missing piece so the output has correct spacing; fix a greeting with a missing space.

knowledge_points.title: Building a string step by step with +=
knowledge_points.worked_example:
msg = ""
msg += "ab"
msg += "cd"
print(msg)   # abcd
knowledge_points.practice: Trace a string variable through several += steps.

knowledge_points.title: + inside print vs commas between values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = "Ada"
print("Hi", name)    # Hi Ada  (print adds a space)
print("Hi" + name)   # HiAda   (+ adds nothing)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which version prints which spacing; rewrite a comma print as one concatenated string.

topics.title: Putting numbers into strings with str()
topics.summary: Fix the str + int TypeError with str(), and convert the other way when strings of digits must be added as numbers.

knowledge_points.title: A string plus a number is a TypeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
age = 30
print("Age: " + age)
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which lines raise TypeError in a short program mixing strings and numbers.

knowledge_points.title: Convert with str() before joining
knowledge_points.worked_example:
age = 30
print("Age: " + str(age))   # Age: 30
knowledge_points.practice: Fix concatenations that mix numbers and text; fill in the conversion.

knowledge_points.title: The other direction: digits as text are joined, not added
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = "3"
b = "4"
print(a + b)             # 34
print(int(a) + int(b))   # 7
knowledge_points.practice: Predict + on strings of digits vs converted numbers; choose the conversion that gives the sum.

knowledge_points.title: Building output from a computed number
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = 9.456
print("Total: " + str(round(total, 2)) + " EUR")
# Total: 9.46 EUR
knowledge_points.practice: Write one line that builds a message from text and a rounded number.

topics.title: Repeating strings with *
topics.summary: Repeat a string with *, combine repetition with +, and avoid the type errors * gives on strings.

knowledge_points.title: A string times an integer repeats it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("ab" * 3)    # ababab
print("-" * 20)    # a line of 20 dashes
knowledge_points.practice: Predict repeated strings; write an expression that makes a line of 10 '='.

knowledge_points.title: Combining * with +
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lines built from * and +; fill in the counts that centre a title in a banner.

knowledge_points.title: Strings vs numbers, and zero repeats
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("3" * 3)   # 333
print(3 * 3)     # 9
print("ab" * 0)  # an empty line: 0 or a negative count gives the empty string ""
knowledge_points.practice: Predict * on digit strings, numbers, and zero or negative counts.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: repeating by a float or a string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
"a" * 2.5   # TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float'
n = "4"
"-" * n     # TypeError; fix with "-" * int(n)
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix repetition bugs caused by a float or an unconverted input string.

topics.title: Getting one character by its index
topics.summary: Read a single character with s[i], counting from 0, and recognise the IndexError for a position past the end.

knowledge_points.title: s[0] is the first character: counting starts at 0
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
print(s[0])   # p
print(s[3])   # h
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the character at given indexes; write the index that picks a named letter.

knowledge_points.title: The last character is at len(s) - 1
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
print(len(s))         # 6
print(s[len(s) - 1])  # n
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the last index of strings of different lengths; write an expression for the last character of any string.

knowledge_points.title: An index past the end raises IndexError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
print(s[6])
# IndexError: string index out of range
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which indexes are valid for a given string; fix an off-by-one that indexes s[len(s)].

knowledge_points.title: Indexes can be variables and expressions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
i = 2
print(s[i], s[i + 1])   # t h
The result is itself a string of length 1.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace i through a few updates and predict s[i] each time.

topics.title: Counting from the end with negative indexes
topics.summary: Use s[-1], s[-2], ... to read characters from the end, and know where negative indexes run out.

knowledge_points.title: s[-1] is the last character
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "code"
print(s[-1])   # e
print(s[-2])   # d
knowledge_points.practice: Predict characters at negative indexes.

knowledge_points.title: Positive and negative indexes name the same positions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
c  o  d  e
 0  1  2  3
-4 -3 -2 -1
s[-k] is s[len(s) - k].
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a table of matching positive and negative indexes; convert between them.

knowledge_points.title: Negative indexes also run out
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "code"
print(s[-4])   # c
print(s[-5])   # IndexError
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which negative indexes are valid for a given length.

knowledge_points.title: Choosing s[-1] over s[len(s) - 1]; empty strings have no last character
knowledge_points.worked_example:
word = "pizza"
print(word[-1])   # a, shorter and clearer
empty = ""
empty[-1]         # IndexError
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite len-based indexes with negative ones; predict which lines fail for an empty string.

topics.title: Slicing a string: s[start:stop]
topics.summary: Take substrings with s[start:stop], including omitted bounds, negative bounds and out-of-range bounds.

knowledge_points.title: s[start:stop] includes start, excludes stop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
print(s[1:4])   # yth: indexes 1, 2, 3
knowledge_points.practice: Predict slices; write the slice that extracts a named part of a word.

knowledge_points.title: A slice has stop - start characters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
print(s[0:3])        # pyt
print(len(s[2:5]))   # 3
knowledge_points.practice: Compute slice lengths; choose bounds that give exactly n characters.

knowledge_points.title: Leaving out start or stop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
print(s[:3])   # pyt  (from the start)
print(s[3:])   # hon  (to the end)
print(s[:])    # python (a full copy)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict slices with omitted bounds; rewrite s[0:len(s)] in its shortest form.

knowledge_points.title: Negative and out-of-range bounds never raise errors
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
print(s[-3:])    # hon
print(s[:-1])    # pytho
print(s[2:100])  # thon, no IndexError
print(s[4:2])    # an empty line: start after stop gives ""
knowledge_points.practice: Predict slices with negative, oversized and crossed bounds; contrast with indexing errors.

topics.title: Slices with a step, and reversing a string
topics.summary: Use s[start:stop:step] to take every n-th character and s[::-1] to reverse a string.

knowledge_points.title: A step skips characters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "abcdefgh"
print(s[::2])    # aceg
print(s[1::2])   # bdfh
knowledge_points.practice: Predict stepped slices; write a slice that takes every third character.

knowledge_points.title: s[::-1] reverses a string
knowledge_points.worked_example: print("stressed"[::-1])   # desserts
knowledge_points.practice: Predict reversed strings; write an expression for a variable's reverse.

knowledge_points.title: Negative step with bounds: start is on the right
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "abcdef"
print(s[4:1:-1])   # edc
print(s[1:4:-1])   # an empty line: with a negative step, start must be after stop
knowledge_points.practice: Predict slices with a negative step and explicit bounds.

knowledge_points.title: Palindrome check with ==
knowledge_points.worked_example:
word = "level"
print(word == word[::-1])   # True
print("abc" == "abc"[::-1])  # False
knowledge_points.practice: Predict palindrome checks; fix a check that compares a string with a slice that drops a character.

topics.title: Common slicing patterns
topics.summary: Take the first or last n characters, trim the ends, split a string at its middle and rebuild strings from slices.

knowledge_points.title: First n and last n characters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "2026-10-12"
n = 2
print(s[:4], s[-n:])   # 2026 12
Careful: s[-0:] is the whole string, not the empty one.
knowledge_points.practice: Write slices for the first/last n characters; predict the n = 0 edge case.

knowledge_points.title: Drop the first and last character
knowledge_points.worked_example:
quoted = '"hi"'
print(quoted[1:-1])   # hi
knowledge_points.practice: Write the slice that strips one character from each end; predict it on 1- and 2-character strings.

knowledge_points.title: Split at the middle with //
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "abcdefg"
mid = len(s) // 2
print(s[:mid], s[mid:])   # abc defg
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the two halves for odd and even lengths.

knowledge_points.title: Rebuild strings from slices with +
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "abcdef"
print(s[2:] + s[:2])          # cdefab (rotate)
print(s[:3] + "-" + s[3:])    # abc-def (insert)
knowledge_points.practice: Write expressions that rotate, insert or remove characters at a position; reorder lines in a Parsons problem.

topics.title: Calling string methods: changing case
topics.summary: Call a method with dot syntax, change case with upper/lower/title/capitalize, store the result, and compare text ignoring case.

knowledge_points.title: Dot syntax: value.method()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = "ada"
print(name.upper())   # ADA
print("HeLLo".lower()) # hello
Without the parentheses, name.upper shows <built-in method ...> instead of calling it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of upper() and lower(); fix a call missing its parentheses.

knowledge_points.title: title(), capitalize() and swapcase()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "ada lovelace"
print(s.title())        # Ada Lovelace
print(s.capitalize())   # Ada lovelace
print("Ab".swapcase())  # aB
knowledge_points.practice: Match each output to the method that produced it.

knowledge_points.title: Methods return a new string: store it to keep it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = "ada"
name.upper()
print(name)          # ada: the result was thrown away
name = name.upper()
print(name)          # ADA
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output when results are or are not stored; fix the missing assignment.

knowledge_points.title: Comparing text while ignoring case
knowledge_points.worked_example:
answer = "Yes"
print(answer == "yes")           # False
print(answer.lower() == "yes")   # True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict comparisons with and without lower(); write a case-insensitive equality check.

topics.title: Trimming with strip(), lstrip() and rstrip()
topics.summary: Remove unwanted spaces, newlines or chosen characters from the ends of a string, and clean up typed answers.

knowledge_points.title: strip() removes whitespace at both ends
knowledge_points.worked_example:
clean = "  hi there \n".strip()
print(clean == "hi there")   # True
Spaces inside the text stay.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict strip() results on strings with leading/trailing spaces, tabs and newlines.

knowledge_points.title: lstrip() and rstrip() trim one side
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "  hi  "
print(s.lstrip() == "hi  ")   # True
print(s.rstrip() == "  hi")   # True
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the method that trims only the side asked for.

knowledge_points.title: strip(chars) removes any of those characters, not a word
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("...hi!!".strip(".!"))       # hi
print("abcHIcba".strip("abc"))     # HI: a, b, c removed in any order
knowledge_points.practice: Predict strip with a character argument, including cases where it removes more than expected.

knowledge_points.title: Cleaning an answer: chain strip() and lower()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
answer = input("Continue? ").strip().lower()
print(answer == "yes")
# user types "  YES " -> True
knowledge_points.practice: Write the cleanup for a typed answer; predict comparisons for messy inputs.

topics.title: Searching inside a string: find(), index() and count()
topics.summary: Locate a substring with find() or index(), handle the not-found case, and count occurrences.

knowledge_points.title: find() returns the index of the first match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("banana".find("an"))   # 1
print("banana".find("x"))    # -1: not found
knowledge_points.practice: Predict find() results, including not-found and matches at index 0.

knowledge_points.title: -1 is not an error, but index() is
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
print(s[s.find("z")])   # n: -1 silently picked the last character
s.index("z")            # ValueError: substring not found
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what happens when a not-found result is used as an index; choose between find and index.

knowledge_points.title: Search from a position, or from the right
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("banana".find("an", 2))   # 3: search starts at index 2
print("banana".rfind("an"))     # 3: last match
knowledge_points.practice: Predict find with a start argument and rfind; write the call that finds the second occurrence.

knowledge_points.title: count() counts non-overlapping matches
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("banana".count("a"))   # 3
print("aaaa".count("aa"))    # 2, not 3
knowledge_points.practice: Predict counts, including overlapping patterns and case differences.

topics.title: Replacing text with replace()
topics.summary: Replace or remove every occurrence of a substring, limit the number of replacements, and avoid order bugs when chaining.

knowledge_points.title: replace(old, new) changes every occurrence
knowledge_points.worked_example: print("a-b-c".replace("-", " "))   # a b c
knowledge_points.practice: Predict replace() results; write a call that turns spaces into underscores.

knowledge_points.title: Remove text by replacing it with ""
knowledge_points.worked_example:
price = "1,000,000".replace(",", "")
print(int(price) + 1)   # 1000001
knowledge_points.practice: Write the cleanup that makes a string convertible with int(); predict the result.

knowledge_points.title: Limit the number of replacements
knowledge_points.worked_example: print("a-b-c".replace("-", " ", 1))   # a b-c
knowledge_points.practice: Predict replace with a count argument.

knowledge_points.title: Case-sensitivity and chaining order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Cat cat".replace("cat", "dog"))   # Cat dog
s = "ab".replace("a", "b").replace("b", "a")
print(s)   # aa: the second replace also hit the new b
knowledge_points.practice: Predict chained replaces; fix a swap that fails because of order.

topics.title: Checking what a string contains: startswith() and the is- methods
topics.summary: Test a string's beginning, end and kind of characters with startswith/endswith and isdigit/isalpha/isalnum/isupper/islower/isspace.

knowledge_points.title: startswith() and endswith()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
f = "report.pdf"
print(f.endswith(".pdf"))     # True
print(f.startswith("Rep"))    # False: case-sensitive
knowledge_points.practice: Predict startswith/endswith results; write a check for a file extension.

knowledge_points.title: isdigit(), isalpha(), isalnum()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("2026".isdigit())   # True
print("-5".isdigit())     # False: - is not a digit
print("3.5".isdigit())    # False
print("ab1".isalnum())    # True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict is- method results on numbers, signs, decimals, spaces and the empty string.

knowledge_points.title: isupper(), islower(), isspace() and the empty string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("A1".isupper())   # True: only letters are checked
print("".isspace())    # False
print("".isdigit())    # False
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results on mixed and empty strings.

knowledge_points.title: Combining checks with and/or
knowledge_points.worked_example:
code = "AB12CD"
print(code.isalnum() and len(code) == 6)   # True
print(code.isdigit() or code.isalpha())    # False
knowledge_points.practice: Write one boolean expression for a validation rule; predict combined checks.

topics.title: Splitting a string into parts with split()
topics.summary: Split text into a list of pieces on whitespace or a separator, read pieces by index, and unpack them into variables.

knowledge_points.title: split() breaks on whitespace
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = "the quick  fox".split()
print(words)        # ['the', 'quick', 'fox']
The result is a list of strings; runs of spaces count as one break.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict split() results on sentences with extra spaces and newlines.

knowledge_points.title: split(sep) breaks on a chosen separator
knowledge_points.practice: Predict split with separators, including empty pieces and leftover spaces.

knowledge_points.title: Reading pieces by index and counting them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
parts = "2026-10-12".split("-")
print(parts[0], parts[-1])   # 2026 12
print(len(parts))            # 3
knowledge_points.practice: Write the expression that picks a given field; count words in a sentence with len(split()).

knowledge_points.title: Unpacking pieces into names
knowledge_points.worked_example:
first, last = "Ada Lovelace".split()
print(last)   # Lovelace
first, last = "Ada King Lovelace".split()   # ValueError: too many values
first, rest = "Ada King Lovelace".split(" ", 1)   # maxsplit fixes it
knowledge_points.practice: Predict unpacking results and errors; fix an unpacking that fails on a three-word name.

topics.title: Joining pieces with join()
topics.summary: Join a list of strings with a separator, normalise spacing with split then join, and fix join on non-strings.

knowledge_points.title: separator.join(pieces)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("-".join(["2026", "10", "12"]))   # 2026-10-12
The separator comes first: ["a", "b"].join("-") is an AttributeError.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict join results; fix a join written the wrong way round.

knowledge_points.title: split() then join(): normalise spaces
knowledge_points.worked_example:
messy = "  too   many    spaces "
print(" ".join(messy.split()))   # too many spaces
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of split-then-join; write the one-liner that collapses extra spaces.

knowledge_points.title: Changing the separator
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(",".join("a b c".split()))   # a,b,c
print("".join("a-b-c".split("-")))   # abc
knowledge_points.practice: Write expressions that convert between separators.

knowledge_points.title: join needs strings
knowledge_points.worked_example:
"-".join(["a", 1])
# TypeError: sequence item 1: expected str instance, int found
"-".join(["a", str(1)])   # a-1
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix joins that include numbers.

topics.title: Extracting parts of text with find() and slicing
topics.summary: Pull a field out of a line of text by finding marker characters and slicing around them.

knowledge_points.title: Text after a marker
knowledge_points.worked_example:
email = "ada@example.com"
at = email.find("@")
print(email[at + 1:])   # example.com
knowledge_points.practice: Write the slice that takes everything after a marker; predict it for several inputs.

knowledge_points.title: Text before a marker
knowledge_points.worked_example:
email = "ada@example.com"
print(email[:email.find("@")])   # ada
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the slice bounds for the part before a marker.

knowledge_points.title: Text between two markers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = "From: <ada@x.org> sent"
start = line.find("<")
end = line.find(">", start)
print(line[start + 1:end])   # ada@x.org
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of an extraction (Parsons); write the extraction for another pair of markers.

knowledge_points.title: Off-by-one and missing-marker bugs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
email = "ada@example.com"
at = email.find("@")
print(email[at:])        # @example.com: forgot + 1
print("ada"["ada".find("@") + 1:])   # ada: -1 + 1 is 0, so no marker means the whole string
knowledge_points.practice: Predict buggy extractions and fix them.

topics.title: f-strings: putting values into text
topics.summary: Write f-strings that insert variables and expressions into text without str(), and avoid the forgotten-f and brace bugs.

knowledge_points.title: f"...{name}..." inserts a value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
print(f"{name} is {age}")   # Ada is 36
No str() needed: numbers are converted for you.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict f-string output; rewrite a + and str() concatenation as an f-string.

knowledge_points.title: Any expression fits in the braces
knowledge_points.practice: Predict f-strings containing arithmetic; fill in the expression that produces a given line.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: forgetting the f
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix strings that print braces literally.

knowledge_points.title: Literal braces: double them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 2
print(f"{{n}} is {n}")   # {n} is 2
knowledge_points.practice: Predict f-strings with doubled braces; write one that prints a brace next to a value.

topics.title: Formatting numbers: decimals, thousands and percentages
topics.summary: Use format specs like :.2f, :, and :.1% to show numbers with fixed decimals, thousands separators and percent signs.

knowledge_points.title: :.2f shows exactly two decimals
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values formatted with .0f, .1f and .2f; write the spec for a price.

knowledge_points.title: Formatting is not rounding the value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 2.0
print(round(x, 2))   # 2.0: round keeps the float as is
print(f"{x:.2f}")    # 2.00: the text is padded
print(x)             # 2.0: x is unchanged
knowledge_points.practice: Choose between round() and a format spec for a given goal; predict both.

knowledge_points.title: Thousands separators with ,
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values formatted with , and ,.2f.

knowledge_points.title: Percentages with %
knowledge_points.worked_example:
part = 32
total = 125
print(f"{part / total:.1%}")   # 25.6%
The % spec multiplies by 100 and adds the sign.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the f-string for a percentage with one decimal; predict .0% results.

topics.title: Lining up output: width, alignment and padding
topics.summary: Give values a minimum width, align them left, right or centre, pad with a fill character or zeros, and print aligned table rows.

knowledge_points.title: A width pads to a minimum size
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = "ada"
print(f"[{name:5}]")   # [ada  ]  strings go left
print(f"[{42:5}]")     # [   42] numbers go right
knowledge_points.practice: Predict padded output for strings and numbers of different lengths.

knowledge_points.title: < > ^ choose the alignment
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = "ada"
print(f"[{name:>5}]")   # [  ada]
print(f"[{name:^7}]")   # [  ada  ]
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the alignment character for a target layout.

knowledge_points.title: Fill characters and zero padding
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = "ada"
print(f"{name:*^9}")   # ***ada***
print(f"{7:03}")        # 007
knowledge_points.practice: Predict fill and zero-padded output; write the spec for a 2-digit minute.

knowledge_points.title: Aligned table rows: width plus decimals
knowledge_points.worked_example:
item = "tea"
price = 2.5
print(f"{item:<8}{price:>7.2f}")
# tea        2.50
knowledge_points.practice: Write the f-string for a receipt row; predict alignment of two rows.

topics.title: Older styles: str.format() and %
topics.summary: Read and write .format() strings and recognise %-formatting, which appear in older code and documentation.

knowledge_points.title: "{} is {}".format(...) fills placeholders in order
knowledge_points.worked_example: print("{} is {}".format("Ada", 36))   # Ada is 36
knowledge_points.practice: Predict .format() output; rewrite an f-string with .format().

knowledge_points.title: Numbered and named placeholders
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("{0} {1} {0}".format("a", "b"))     # a b a
print("{n} items".format(n=3))          # 3 items
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output with reused and named placeholders.

knowledge_points.title: The same format specs work in .format()
knowledge_points.practice: Translate f-string specs to .format() and back.

knowledge_points.title: Recognising %-formatting
knowledge_points.practice: Match %-style strings with their f-string equivalents.

topics.title: Strings cannot be changed: build new ones
topics.summary: Recognise that strings are immutable, build a modified copy with slicing and +, and tell reassigning a name apart from changing a string.

knowledge_points.title: Assigning to an index is a TypeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
s[0] = "J"
# TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which lines fail in programs that read or assign string indexes.

knowledge_points.title: Build a new string from slices
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "python"
s = "J" + s[1:]
print(s)   # Jython
knowledge_points.practice: Write expressions that replace the character at a given index; fix an item-assignment bug.

knowledge_points.title: Reassigning a name is not changing the string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a = "hi"
b = a
a += "!"
print(a, b)   # hi! hi
a now names a new string; b still names the old one.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace two names through reassignments and predict the output.

knowledge_points.title: Every method returns a new string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "a-b"
s.replace("-", "+")
s.upper()
print(s)   # a-b: both results were discarded
s = s.replace("-", "+").upper()   # A+B
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix programs where method results are not stored.

topics.title: Characters are numbers: ord() and chr()
topics.summary: Convert between characters and their Unicode code points, explain string ordering, and shift letters with wrap-around.

knowledge_points.title: ord() gives a character's code, chr() goes back
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(ord("A"), ord("a"), ord(" "))   # 65 97 32
print(chr(66))                         # B
ord("ab") is a TypeError: one character only.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict ord/chr results for letters, digits and spaces.

knowledge_points.title: Letters and digits have consecutive codes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(chr(ord("a") + 1))        # b
print(ord("z") - ord("a"))      # 25
print(ord("7") - ord("0"))      # 7
knowledge_points.practice: Compute a letter's position in the alphabet; predict the character n places later.

knowledge_points.title: Codes explain string ordering
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Zoo" < "apple")      # True
print(ord("Z"), ord("a"))   # 90 97: every capital comes before every lowercase letter
knowledge_points.practice: Predict string comparisons by comparing first-character codes.

knowledge_points.title: Shifting a letter with wrap-around (Caesar shift)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
c = "y"
shifted = chr((ord(c) - ord("a") + 3) % 26 + ord("a"))
print(shifted)   # b
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the steps of a shift (Parsons); predict shifts that wrap past z.

topics.title: Unicode text and bytes: encode() and decode()
topics.summary: Handle non-English characters, convert text to UTF-8 bytes and back, and recognise encoding errors and garbled text.

knowledge_points.title: A string can hold any Unicode character
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = "café ☕"
print(len(s))           # 6: one per character
print("\u00e9" == "é")  # True: \u gives a character by its code
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() and ord() on accented letters and symbols.

knowledge_points.title: encode() turns text into bytes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
b = "café".encode("utf-8")
print(b)        # b'caf\xc3\xa9'
print(len(b))   # 5: é takes two bytes in UTF-8
knowledge_points.practice: Predict byte lengths of encoded strings; tell a str from a bytes value by its b prefix.

knowledge_points.title: decode() turns bytes back into text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
b = b"caf\xc3\xa9"
print(b.decode("utf-8"))   # café
knowledge_points.practice: Write the round trip text -> bytes -> text.

knowledge_points.title: The wrong encoding: errors and garbled text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
"café".encode("ascii")           # UnicodeEncodeError
b"caf\xc3\xa9".decode("latin-1")  # 'cafÃ©': wrong codec, garbled text
knowledge_points.practice: Diagnose which encoding mistake produced an error or garbled output.
